Hello! I was working through a proof for something of a side project of mine, not work or school related and I appear to be stuck at a point where I don't know if something exists yet or not. Forgive me if I am doing this incorrectly here, I did read the guidelines so hopefully this is ok to ask here.

What I can't find the answer to yet:
I need to prove that the sum of N-th roots of unity is zero.
∑ i : Fin N, ω ^ (i : ℕ) = 0
where ω = Complex.exp (-2 * Real.pi * Complex.I * k / N) and k : Fin N with k ≠ 0

Is there something in Mathlib I can use for this proof or what would the suggested approach perhaps be for this problem?

Thank you!
-Tim

import Mathlib

open Complex Real

example (N : ℕ) (hN : 1 < N) (k : Fin N) (hk : (k : ℕ) ≠ 0) :
    ∑ i : Fin N, Complex.exp (-2 * π * I * k / N) ^ (i : ℕ) = 0 := by
  replace hN : (N : ℂ) ≠ 0 := by norm_cast; omega
  rw [mul_comm, ← mul_div, Complex.exp_nat_mul, ← Finset.sum_range, geom_sum_eq]
  · convert zero_div _
    rw [sub_eq_zero, ← Complex.exp_nat_mul, ← Complex.exp_nat_mul]
    field_simp
    rw [Complex.exp_neg, inv_eq_one, Complex.exp_eq_one_iff]
    use k
    simp
    ring
  · intro h
    rw [neg_mul, neg_mul, neg_div, ← Complex.exp_nat_mul, mul_neg, Complex.exp_neg, inv_eq_one] at h
    obtain ⟨n, hn⟩ := Complex.exp_eq_one_iff.1 h
    rw [← mul_div_assoc, mul_comm, mul_comm (n : ℂ), mul_div_assoc] at hn
    simp only [mul_eq_mul_left_iff, mul_eq_zero, OfNat.ofNat_ne_zero, ofReal_eq_zero, pi_ne_zero,
      or_self, I_ne_zero, or_false] at hn
    rw [div_eq_iff hN] at hn
    norm_cast at hn
    lift n to ℕ
    · by_contra! H
      suffices n * N ≤ 0 by
        grind
      grw [H]
      simp
    · suffices N ≤ k by
        grind
      norm_cast at hn
      rw [hn]
      refine Nat.le_mul_of_pos_left N ?_
      grind
We should have a version of Complex.exp_eq_one_iff that gives a natural number instead of an integer.

Here is my version. The helper lemma is a bit annoying...

import Mathlib

open Complex Real

lemma foo {N : ℕ} {k : Fin N} (hk : (k : ℕ) ≠ 0) (hN' : (N : ℂ) ≠ 0) :
    cexp (-(2 * π * I * k) / N) ≠ 1 := by
  simp only [ne_eq]
  rw [Complex.exp_eq_one_iff]
  push Not
  intro n
  rw [ne_eq, neg_div, neg_eq_iff_eq_neg]
  field_simp
  norm_cast
  have hk₁ : N * 0 < (k : ℤ) := by grind
  have hk₂ : (k : ℤ) < N * 1 := by grind
  intro H
  rw [Int.neg_mul_eq_mul_neg] at H
  rw [H, ← nsmul_eq_mul, ← nsmul_eq_mul] at hk₁ hk₂
  grind [lt_of_nsmul_lt_nsmul_right N hk₁, lt_of_nsmul_lt_nsmul_right N hk₂]

example (N : ℕ) (hN : 1 < N) (k : Fin N) (hk : (k : ℕ) ≠ 0) :
    ∑ i : Fin N, Complex.exp (-2 * π * I * k / N) ^ (i : ℕ) = 0 := by
  simp only [Finset.sum_fin_eq_sum_range, neg_mul, dite_eq_ite]
  have hN' : (N : ℂ) ≠ 0 := by norm_cast; lia
  rw [Finset.sum_ite_of_true (by simp), geom_sum_eq (foo hk hN'), ← Complex.exp_nat_mul]
  field_simp
  rw [show -(2 * ↑π * I * ↑↑k) = (-k : ℤ) * (2 * π * I) by push_cast; ring, exp_int_mul_two_pi_mul_I]
  simp

Just an update. In case this might help someone else in the future, this is what I proved just now with everyones help.

DFT_const_zero is now fully proved with no sorries.

Theorem shows that DFT of a constant signal is zero at all non zero frequencies which I needed in order to move toward a proof of the Parseval's theorem. I am just sharing this now in case someone might find it useful for future work.

Here is the result code:

import Mathlib

open BigOperators Real Nat Complex


/-- DFT of a constant signal: if x(n) = c for all n,
    then X(0) = N * c and X(k) = 0 for k ≠ 0 -/
theorem DFT_const_zero (N : ℕ) (hN : 1 < N) (c : ℂ) (k : Fin N)
    (hk : (k : ℕ) ≠ 0) :
    DFT N (fun _ => c) k = 0 := by
  simp only [DFT]
  have hN' : (N : ℂ) ≠ 0 := by norm_cast; omega
  have hbase : ∀ x : Fin N, c * Complex.exp (-2 * Real.pi * Complex.I
      * (k : ℂ) * (x : ℂ) / (N : ℂ)) =
      c * Complex.exp (-2 * Real.pi * Complex.I * (k : ℂ) / (N : ℂ)) ^ (x : ℕ) := by
    intro x
    rw [← Complex.exp_nat_mul]
    congr 1
    push_cast
    ring
  simp_rw [hbase, ← Finset.mul_sum]
  apply mul_eq_zero_of_right
  set x := Complex.exp (-2 * Real.pi * Complex.I * (k : ℂ) / (N : ℂ))
  have hx_pow_N : x ^ N = 1 := by
    simp only [x]
    rw [← Complex.exp_nat_mul]
    have : (N : ℂ) * (-2 * Real.pi * Complex.I * k / N) =
        -(2 * Real.pi * Complex.I * k) := by field_simp
    rw [this]
    rw [show -(2 * Real.pi * Complex.I * (k : ℂ)) =
        (-↑(k : ℕ) : ℤ) * (2 * Real.pi * Complex.I) by push_cast; ring]
    exact Complex.exp_int_mul_two_pi_mul_I _
  have hx_ne_one : x ≠ 1 := by
    simp only [x, ne_eq]
    rw [show -2 * Real.pi * Complex.I * (k : ℂ) / N =
        -(2 * Real.pi * Complex.I * k) / N by ring]
    exact dft_base_ne_one hk (by norm_cast; omega)
  have hsum : ∑ i : Fin N, x ^ (i : ℕ) =
      ∑ i ∈ Finset.range N, x ^ i := by
    rw [Finset.sum_fin_eq_sum_range]
    apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
    intro i hi
    simp [Finset.mem_range.mp hi]
  rw [hsum, geom_sum_eq hx_ne_one, hx_pow_N]
  simp

You shouldn't need hN as a hypothesis (it's implied by hk).

@Yaël Dillies it seems that you are doing the number-theoretic-transforms as well? Your REAMDE calls it Discrete Fourier Transform but I've never seen the term DFT used to refer to something using finite fields (although it's also used that way by Wikipedia). Rather, it usually refers to a transform Cn→Cn\mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{C}^nCn→Cn .

Are you planning to touch on Cooley-Turkey-like FFT algorithms? The README suggests that this is not the focus, so I assume not?

The discrete Fourier transform is simply the Fourier transform on a discrete group, so that it can be expressed as a (possibly infinite) sum. Anyway, I have come to realise that I was being misled by my groups being finite (ie compact and discrete), and that in fact the Fourier transform I care about is the compact Fourier transform, ie the Fourier transform from a compact group, which can be expressed as an average. Over a finite group, it is the same as the discrete one, up to a factor of the size of the group
I have no plans to implement or prove correct any FFT-style algorithm

and want to give a try. I just want to know if any of you is working on the same thing. If so, I'll go do something else.

@Ching-Tsun Chou I've been doing a version of NTT with AI (with the idea that "I write down the equation I want, the AI writes an appropriate variant of the "fast" NTT algorithm, and then proves that it equals the equation"). I don't even really understand the exact "fast" algorithm variant it's doing (radix 4 using Montgomery multiplication), which I chose by means of benchmarking speed, and I'm using it to implement convolution of vectors in GF(2)\mathrm{GF}(2)GF(2) (a rare application, I guess).

All in all, the proofs I have are super ugly and it's more of an AI experiment rather than an attempt to write something pedagogically meaningful or a human-reusable library.

If you're interested, I can put the code I have on GitHub (a small part of the proof is still sorry but I expect that the AI will probably finish it this week). Apart from that, I personally wouldn't want anyone interested in related formalization (or even the exact one I'm doing) to stop just because I'm already doing it.
